stem: a case of epistaxis.. What is the most appropriate position?
key_concept:
Epistaxis first aid: sit up, lean forward, pinch the soft nose.
  • Continuous pressure on the soft part of the nose (not the bony bridge) for at least 10 to 15 minutes
  • Spit out blood, do not swallow; ice to the nose or mouth may help
  • Persisting: topical vasoconstrictor, cautery of a visible anterior bleeding point
  • Still bleeding: anterior packing; suspected posterior bleed: posterior packing or balloon and admission
  • Check hemodynamics in heavy bleeding
exam_pearl: Leaning back is the classic wrong instinct; forward lean keeps blood out of the airway and stomach.

stem: A child had an URTI for 4 days (clear nasal discharge, fever, sneezing); 3 days after resolving of the symptoms he presented with purulent nasal discharge and frontal tenderness. What's the diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: purulent nasal discharge and frontal tenderness
why_right: The pattern is double worsening: a viral URTI ("clear nasal discharge, fever, sneezing") settles, then the child deteriorates again with purulent nasal discharge and frontal tenderness. A new worsening after initial improvement, with sinus tenderness, is a classic criterion for acute bacterial sinusitis secondary to the viral illness.
why_wrong_block:
A. Viral URTI explains the first 4 days, but it does not recur after resolution with purulent discharge and sinus tenderness. Right when symptoms are under about 10 days and steadily improving.
C. Allergic rhinosinusitis gives clear watery discharge, sneezing and itch, often seasonal or with triggers, without fever or purulent discharge. Right in a child with recurrent itchy rhinorrhoea and an atopic background.
D. The second episode is directly linked to the URTI: viral mucosal swelling blocks sinus drainage and allows secondary bacterial infection, so calling it unrelated misses the diagnosis.
key_concept:
Suspect acute bacterial sinusitis after a URTI when one of three patterns occurs:
  • Persistent: nasal discharge or cough lasting ≥10 days without improvement
  • Severe onset: high fever with purulent discharge for several days
  • Double worsening: new fever or worse discharge after initial improvement (this card)
  • Clear watery discharge with sneezing and itch: allergic
exam_pearl: Purulent discharge alone does not mean bacterial; it is the timing (persistence or worsening after improvement) that flips viral to bacterial.

stem: Child with 4 recurrent adenotonsillitis within one academic year, his parents worried bc it affects his school attendance. What to do??
OptD: Avoid outdoor activities during cold season
highlight_terms_source: 4 recurrent adenotonsillitis within one academic year
why_right: 4 episodes in one academic year is below the threshold for tonsillectomy (≥7 in 1 year, ≥5 per year for 2 years, or ≥3 per year for 3 years), so the child is managed by watchful waiting and prevention. Most episodes are transmitted by droplets and hands at school, so hand washing and respiratory etiquette is the appropriate advice to the worried parents.
why_wrong_block:
A. Tonsillectomy is considered only when the Paradise frequency criteria are met (or with obstruction, peritonsillar abscess, PFAPA); 4 episodes in a year does not qualify.
B. Prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended for recurrent tonsillitis; they offer little benefit and promote resistance and adverse effects.
D. Avoiding outdoor activity does not prevent infection; spread occurs indoors through close contact, and restricting activity harms the child without benefit.
key_concept:
Recurrent tonsillitis: count episodes before deciding.
  • Paradise criteria for tonsillectomy: ≥7 in 1 year, ≥5 per year for 2 years, ≥3 per year for 3 years
  • Each episode documented (fever, exudate, cervical nodes, or positive strep test)
  • Below threshold: watchful waiting, hygiene, treat each episode
  • Other indications: obstructive sleep disordered breathing, recurrent peritonsillar abscess
exam_pearl: School absence makes parents push for surgery, but frequency below Paradise criteria means watchful waiting and hygiene.

stem: A 40 years old man presented with profuse nosebleeding over 30 minutes, he has a history of recurrent nasal congestion. He is known case of hypertension. On examination he was pale and anxious. Dx?
OptC: Posterior epistaxis due to hypertensive vasculopathy
why_right: A 40 year old known hypertensive with profuse bleeding over 30 minutes that leaves him pale and anxious fits posterior epistaxis from the sphenopalatine artery branches, typical of older adults with hypertension and vascular disease. Anterior (Little's area) bleeds are usually minor and stop with pressure; heavy, prolonged bleeding in a hypertensive adult points posteriorly. Recurrent nasal congestion is a nonspecific background detail.
why_wrong_block:
A. Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma occurs in adolescent males, presenting with unilateral nasal obstruction and recurrent profuse epistaxis; it is not a diagnosis for a 40 year old man.
B. Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia causes recurrent epistaxis from childhood with mucocutaneous telangiectasias (lips, tongue, fingers) and a family history; none are described.
D. Coagulopathy related epistaxis would need anticoagulant or antiplatelet use, liver disease or a bleeding disorder history with bleeding at other sites; the only risk factor given is hypertension.
key_concept:
Epistaxis: anterior vs posterior.
  • Anterior (about 90%): Little's area (Kiesselbach plexus), children and young adults, trauma, dry air; stops with pressure
  • Posterior: sphenopalatine artery branches, older adults with hypertension and atherosclerosis, heavy bleeding into the pharynx, hard to control
  • Posterior management: resuscitate, posterior packing or balloon, admit; endoscopic sphenopalatine ligation if refractory
  • Adolescent male with nasal obstruction plus epistaxis: angiofibroma
  • Telangiectasias plus family history: HHT
exam_pearl: Same profuse epistaxis in a teenage boy with nasal obstruction flips the answer to angiofibroma.

stem: A child presents with foul-smelling breath, nasal congestion, and facial tenderness. The symptoms have worsened after 14 days, despite multiple courses of antibiotics. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
highlight_terms_source: worsened after 14 days, despite multiple courses of antibiotics
why_right: Sinus symptoms with foul smelling breath that have worsened after 14 days despite multiple antibiotic courses mean refractory sinusitis: more antibiotics blindly is not the answer. Nasal endoscopy allows direct inspection for a cause (nasal foreign body, adenoid hypertrophy, polyps, anatomic obstruction) and an endoscopically guided culture to direct therapy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Plain sinus X-ray is no longer recommended for sinusitis; it has poor sensitivity and specificity. When imaging is needed in refractory or complicated cases, CT is the modality.
B. Another empirical antibiotic course is right for a first treatment failure; after multiple failed courses the cause and organism must be identified first.
key_concept:
Sinusitis not responding to antibiotics: look for the reason.
  • One failure at 72 h: broaden to amoxicillin clavulanate
  • Multiple failures: nasal endoscopy with culture, CT sinuses
  • Unilateral foul discharge or foul breath in a child: nasal foreign body
  • Recurrent or chronic in children: adenoid hypertrophy, allergy, cystic fibrosis, immunodeficiency
  • Eye or neuro signs: contrast CT and IV antibiotics
exam_pearl: Refractory to several antibiotic courses means find the cause (endoscopy or CT), not another antibiotic.

stem: A 5-year-old child came with SOB was playing with coins. X ray: a coin in the trachea. Definitive management?
why_right: A child "playing with coins" who now has "SOB" and an X-ray showing "a coin in the trachea" has a confirmed airway foreign body. The definitive management is removal under general anaesthesia by rigid bronchoscopy, which both confirms the object and extracts it in the same procedure. A tracheal foreign body can shift and cause complete obstruction, so it is never left to pass.
why_wrong_block:
A. Reassurance: acceptable only for a low risk object already past the oesophagus into the stomach in a well child; an airway foreign body with breathlessness is an emergency.
B. Observation: used for a smooth coin in the stomach or lower oesophagus in an asymptomatic child; aspirated objects do not clear on their own and can cause sudden total obstruction.
C. Serial X-rays: track the passage of a swallowed (GI) coin; a coin in the airway will not move distally, and waiting delays removal.
key_concept:
Airway foreign body = rigid bronchoscopy (diagnostic and therapeutic).
  • Coin in trachea: seen edge on (sagittal) on AP film; coin in oesophagus: seen face on (en face)
  • Radiolucent FB: look for unilateral hyperinflation with mediastinal shift away on expiratory film
  • Negative X-ray does not exclude aspiration; strong history still needs bronchoscopy
  • Swallowed coin in stomach, child well: observe, serial X-rays
  • Button battery in oesophagus: urgent removal
exam_pearl: Trap: "serial X-rays" and "observation" belong to swallowed coins in the GI tract, not to a coin in the airway.

stem: Patient with severe hypertension and anterior epistaxis while on aspirin. Imaging normal. Most appropriate next step?
why_right: "Anterior epistaxis" with "imaging normal" needs the bleeding point identified and controlled locally, so the next step is nasal examination with endoscopy (after first aid pressure) to find the source, usually Little's area, and treat it with cautery or packing. "Severe hypertension" and "aspirin" make bleeding harder to stop, but they are managed alongside local control, not instead of it.
why_wrong_block:
A. Facial CT: reserved for suspected tumour, trauma with fracture, or unexplained recurrent posterior bleeds; imaging is already normal and does not stop the bleed.
B. Refer to cardiology: blood pressure is controlled in parallel (analgesia, anxiolysis, antihypertensives if needed), but referral leaves the active nosebleed untreated.
key_concept:
Epistaxis ladder: ABC and first aid, then localise, then control.
  • First aid: sit up, lean forward, firm pressure on the soft nose
  • Anterior rhinoscopy or nasal endoscopy to locate the bleeding point
  • Visible anterior point: chemical (silver nitrate) or electric cautery
  • Not controlled or not seen: anterior nasal packing
  • Persistent or posterior bleed: posterior packing or balloon, ENT, consider vessel ligation or embolisation
  • Correct contributors alongside: hypertension, antiplatelets, coagulopathy
exam_pearl: Hypertension and aspirin are contributors to control in parallel; the next step is still to find and treat the bleeding point.

stem: A pediatric patient presented with ear discharge, high-grade fever, and other symptoms. What is the most likely cause?
why_right: A child with "ear discharge" and "high-grade fever" fits acute otitis media with a perforated, discharging drum. In pediatric acute otitis media the most common causative class is bacterial, led by Streptococcus pneumoniae, then nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis. Viruses often precede it but the purulent middle ear infection itself is mostly bacterial.
why_wrong_block:
A. Viral: viruses (rhinovirus is the most common viral agent) trigger eustachian tube dysfunction and often precede AOM, but purulent otorrhoea with high fever points to bacterial infection; pick rhinovirus only when every option is a virus.
B. Fungal: otomycosis (Aspergillus, Candida) is an outer ear infection with itch and fluffy debris, often after topical antibiotics, usually without high fever.
D. Parasitic: not a recognised cause of otitis media; aural myiasis or a live insect in the canal is a foreign body problem, not an infection with fever and discharge.
key_concept:
Pediatric AOM: bacterial is the most common class.
  • Top bacterium: Streptococcus pneumoniae
  • Others: nontypeable H. influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis
  • Top virus: rhinovirus
  • Otitis externa: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus
  • First line antibiotic for AOM: amoxicillin
exam_pearl: If the options list only viruses, the answer becomes rhinovirus; if they list classes, it is bacterial.

stem: kid with 4 episodes of tonsillitis, missed a few days from school now doing well
OptB: don’t play out in the cold
why_right: "4 episodes of tonsillitis" with a child "now doing well" does not meet the frequency threshold for tonsillectomy, so management is conservative: watchful waiting and prevention of spread. Hand hygiene is the simplest and most effective measure to reduce transmission of the viral and streptococcal infections behind recurrent tonsillitis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Tonsillectomy: indicated when episodes are frequent enough (Paradise criteria: at least 7 in 1 year, 5 per year for 2 years, or 3 per year for 3 years) or with complications such as peritonsillar abscess or obstructive sleep apnoea; 4 episodes is below this.
B. Don't play out in the cold: a myth; cold exposure does not cause tonsillitis, which spreads by droplets and contact.
D. Prophylactic antibiotics: not recommended for recurrent tonsillitis; long term penicillin prophylaxis is for secondary prevention of rheumatic fever.
key_concept:
Recurrent tonsillitis below the threshold: watchful waiting plus hygiene.
  • Paradise criteria: ≥7 episodes in 1 year, ≥5 per year for 2 years, or ≥3 per year for 3 years
  • Other indications: peritonsillar abscess, obstructive sleep apnoea from tonsillar hypertrophy, suspected malignancy
  • Penicillin prophylaxis: rheumatic fever, not recurrent sore throat
  • Hand hygiene: best simple measure against spread of infection
exam_pearl: Count the episodes: fewer than the Paradise numbers means no surgery, even if school is missed.

stem: 10 year old boy with frontal headache, fever, and stuffed nose. 2 days prior he had runny nose and sore throat. On examination, he had left cheek tenderness. What is the next best management?
highlight_terms_source: frontal headache, fever, and stuffed nose
key_concept:
Sinusitis in children is decided by timeline and severity, not by imaging.
  • Early (within days of a cold), mild: viral, supportive care
  • Persistent > 10 days without improvement: bacterial, antibiotics
  • Double sickening (worse after improving): bacterial
  • Severe onset (high fever with purulent discharge for ≥3 days): bacterial
  • Antibiotic: amoxicillin, or amoxicillin clavulanate if risk of resistance
  • Imaging (CT) only for orbital or intracranial complications
exam_pearl: Cheek tenderness alone does not make it bacterial; the duration and pattern of illness decide antibiotics.

stem: 7 Years old complains of chronic clear thin nasal discharge and easy nasal itching, o/e there is periorbital dark swollen and pale turbinates mucosa. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A child with "chronic clear thin nasal discharge" and "nasal itching", with "periorbital dark swollen" skin (allergic shiners) and "pale turbinates mucosa", has the classic picture of allergic rhinitis. Itch, watery discharge, bilateral symptoms and pale boggy mucosa are the atopic signature.
why_wrong_block:
B. Foreign body: gives unilateral, foul smelling, purulent or bloody discharge in a young child; this child has bilateral clear discharge with itch.
C. TB: rare nasal cause with crusting, ulceration or granulomas and systemic features; not chronic itchy watery rhinorrhoea.
D. Rhinitis medicamentosa: rebound congestion from prolonged topical decongestant use, with red swollen mucosa; there is no history of decongestant spray overuse here.
key_concept:
Allergic rhinitis: itch + clear rhinorrhoea + pale boggy turbinates.
  • Signs: allergic shiners (dark infraorbital swelling), nasal crease (allergic salute), Dennie Morgan lines
  • Associated atopy: asthma, eczema, allergic conjunctivitis
  • Unilateral foul discharge in a child: foreign body
  • Rebound congestion after decongestant sprays: rhinitis medicamentosa
  • First line for persistent symptoms: intranasal corticosteroid
exam_pearl: Unilateral foul discharge flips the answer to foreign body; bilateral clear itchy discharge stays allergic.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler note on option B: it was written foreign “boy” in the exam.

stem: A 10 year old came 5 days post tonsillectomy with bleeding. Which of the following is the cause?
why_right: Bleeding "5 days post tonsillectomy" is a secondary haemorrhage (after 24 hours, typically days 5 to 10), classically attributed to infection of the tonsillar fossa and separation of the slough. Primary haemorrhage (within 24 hours) is the one blamed on surgical technique, such as an unsecured vessel.
why_wrong_block:
A. Foreign body: not a recognised cause of post tonsillectomy bleeding; it would cause local trauma or obstruction, not a typical day 5 bleed.
C. Incomplete resection: residual tonsil tissue leads to regrowth or recurrent symptoms, not a timed secondary bleed; early technical problems give primary haemorrhage within 24 hours.
D. Coagulopathy: would usually cause bleeding during or soon after surgery (primary haemorrhage) and is screened for preoperatively; think of it when bleeding is intraoperative or from multiple sites.
key_concept:
Post tonsillectomy haemorrhage is classified by timing.
  • Primary: within 24 hours, surgical technique (unsecured vessel)
  • Secondary: after 24 hours, usually days 5 to 10, infection and slough separation
  • Management: assess airway and resuscitate, ENT review, antibiotics, return to theatre if bleeding persists
exam_pearl: Timing flips the cause: within 24 hours think surgical technique; around day 5 to 10 think infection.

stem: child with allergic rhinitis still sneezing and nasal cognition even after take antihistamine:
why_right: A child with allergic rhinitis "still sneezing" with nasal congestion "even after" an antihistamine needs step up to an intranasal corticosteroid, the most effective single drug for allergic rhinitis and the best for congestion, which antihistamines treat poorly. It is first line for persistent or moderate to severe symptoms in children.
why_wrong_block:
B. Montelukast: less effective than an intranasal corticosteroid for rhinitis; consider it mainly when coexisting asthma is present or as an add on, with attention to its neuropsychiatric side effects.
C. Oral decongestant: only short term symptomatic relief with systemic side effects, and not recommended in young children; it does not treat the allergic inflammation.
D. Allergy immunotherapy: for symptoms uncontrolled despite optimal drugs including intranasal steroids, with a proven specific allergen; it is not the next step after antihistamine alone.
key_concept:
Allergic rhinitis ladder in children.
  • Allergen avoidance and saline irrigation
  • Mild intermittent: oral or intranasal antihistamine
  • Persistent, moderate to severe, or congestion predominant: intranasal corticosteroid
  • Still uncontrolled: combine intranasal steroid with intranasal antihistamine; consider montelukast if asthma coexists
  • Refractory with a proven allergen: allergen immunotherapy
exam_pearl: Congestion that persists on antihistamine points to the intranasal steroid; immunotherapy comes only after optimal drug therapy fails.

stem: Boy complains of URTI, treated. 2 weeks later comes with itchy nose, and congestion on examination there is tenderness on the frontal cheeks . What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: Nasal symptoms continuing "2 weeks later" after a URTI, now with congestion and facial tenderness over the cheeks, fit acute bacterial sinusitis: symptoms lasting beyond 10 days without resolution plus sinus tenderness. The key clues are the preceding URTI and the timeline, which favour a bacterial complication over a new allergic process.
why_wrong_block:
B. Allergic rhinitis: chronic or seasonal itch, sneezing and clear discharge with pale mucosa and atopy, without sinus tenderness; the itchy nose here is a distractor.
C. Foreign body obstruction: unilateral, foul smelling discharge in a young child, unrelated to a preceding URTI.
D. Nasal polyps: grey glistening masses with chronic obstruction and reduced smell; uncommon in children unless cystic fibrosis is present, and they do not cause cheek tenderness after a cold.
key_concept:
Post URTI symptoms beyond 10 days = suspect bacterial sinusitis.
  • Bacterial pattern: persistent > 10 days, double sickening, or severe onset with high fever
  • Maxillary tenderness over the cheeks supports sinus involvement
  • Common organisms: S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis
  • Treatment: amoxicillin or amoxicillin clavulanate
  • Nasal polyps in a child: screen for cystic fibrosis
exam_pearl: Timing beats itch: a URTI that drags on past 10 days with facial tenderness is sinusitis, not allergy.

stem: child had an URTI for 4 days (he has clear nasal discharge, fever, sneezing) , 3 days after resolving of the symptoms he presented with purulent nasal discharge and frontal tenderness. What's the diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: 3 days after resolving of the symptoms
purulent nasal discharge and frontal tenderness
why_right: The pattern is double worsening: a viral URTI ("clear nasal discharge, fever, sneezing") settles, then the child deteriorates again with purulent nasal discharge and frontal tenderness. A new worsening after initial improvement, with sinus tenderness, is a classic criterion for acute bacterial sinusitis secondary to the viral illness.

A. Viral URTI explains the first 4 days, but it does not recur after resolution with purulent discharge and sinus tenderness. Right when symptoms are under about 10 days and steadily improving.
C. Allergic rhinosinusitis gives clear watery discharge, sneezing and itch, often seasonal or with triggers, without fever or purulent discharge. Right in a child with recurrent itchy rhinorrhoea and an atopic background.
D. The second episode is directly linked to the URTI: viral mucosal swelling blocks sinus drainage and allows secondary bacterial infection, so calling it unrelated misses the diagnosis.
key_concept:
Suspect acute bacterial sinusitis after a URTI when one of three patterns occurs:
  • Persistent: nasal discharge or cough lasting ≥10 days without improvement
  • Severe onset: high fever with purulent discharge for several days
  • Double worsening: new fever or worse discharge after initial improvement (this card)
  • Clear watery discharge with sneezing and itch: allergic
exam_pearl: Purulent discharge alone does not mean bacterial; it is the timing (persistence or worsening after improvement) that flips viral to bacterial.

stem: A 45-year-old diabetic man presented with dull aching headache increases with straining and coughing, there is tenderness all over the eyebrows. What is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: dull aching headache increases with straining and coughing
why_right: A dull aching headache that increases with straining and coughing plus tenderness over the eyebrows (frontal sinus area) is typical of frontal sinusitis: raising sinus pressure (coughing, straining, bending forward) worsens the pain and the overlying bone is tender. There is no fever pattern, neck stiffness, confusion or focal deficit to suggest a CNS infection.
why_wrong_block:
A. Viral meningitis presents with acute fever, headache, photophobia and neck stiffness, not localized tenderness over the eyebrows. Right in a febrile patient with meningism and a lymphocytic CSF with normal glucose.
B. TB meningitis is a subacute illness over weeks with low-grade fever, cranial nerve palsies, confusion and a lymphocytic CSF with high protein and low glucose. Nothing here suggests it.
C. Brain abscess headache can also worsen with coughing (raised intracranial pressure), but it brings fever, focal neurological deficits, seizures or vomiting, and no superficial sinus tenderness. It is a complication to consider if sinusitis is followed by neurological signs.
key_concept:
Headache plus local sinus tenderness = sinusitis until proven otherwise.
  • Frontal sinus: tenderness above the eyebrows
  • Maxillary sinus: cheek tenderness, upper tooth pain
  • Pain worse with bending, coughing or straining
  • Red flags (periorbital swelling, diplopia, focal signs, altered consciousness) suggest orbital or intracranial spread
exam_pearl: A diabetic with sinus symptoms plus black nasal eschar or facial necrosis is mucormycosis, an emergency; without those features it is simple sinusitis.

stem: 7 y old boy with fever, cough (Symptoms of pneumonia), PE show localized left lower consolidation. O2 is 94. "He can drink fluids" (written exactly). What is the most appropriate step?
OptA: Admit for IV antibiotics and x ray
OptB: Discharge on oral amoxicillin with clear instructions
OptC: Discharge on oral macrolide with follow up in clinic
why_right: This is mild community-acquired pneumonia in a stable child: localized consolidation, saturation 94% (not hypoxaemic) and the key line "he can drink fluids", meaning he tolerates oral intake. A stable child who can take orally is treated as an outpatient, and oral amoxicillin is the first-line antibiotic because Streptococcus pneumoniae is the main target. Clear return instructions (safety-netting) complete the plan.
why_wrong_block:
A. Admission for IV antibiotics is for severe disease: hypoxaemia, respiratory distress, toxic look, inability to drink, complications such as effusion, or failed oral therapy. The stem stresses he can drink and saturation is 94%, and a chest X-ray is not routinely needed for a mild, clinically clear case managed at home.
C. Macrolides cover atypical organisms such as Mycoplasma, which become common from school age but are suggested by gradual onset, diffuse or bilateral signs and extrapulmonary features. Focal lobar consolidation points to pneumococcus, so amoxicillin stays first line even at 7 years.
key_concept:
Pediatric CAP: decide outpatient vs admission by severity, not by the diagnosis itself.
  • Stable, oxygenating, drinking: oral amoxicillin at home with safety-netting
  • Admit: hypoxaemia, moderate to severe distress, unable to keep hydrated, toxic, complicated pneumonia, early infancy
  • Macrolide: when atypical pneumonia is suspected
exam_pearl: "Can drink fluids" is the deciding clue; if the stem says vomiting everything or refusing feeds, the answer flips to admission.

stem: A 3-year-old child seen in the clinic with fever and cough for 5 days following flu-like prodrome. On examination, he had decrease air entry and crackles over right lung middle zone. Chest X-ray is done (see image and lab results). Blood pressure 90/64 mmHg, Heart rate 110 /min, Respiratory rate 20 /min, Temperature 36.6 °C, Oxygen saturation 97 %. Hb 12 (165-195 g/L newborn; 112-165 g/L child), Platelets 328 (150-400 x 10^9/L), Neutrophils 80 (40-60%), WBC 22 (4.5-13.5 x 10^9/L 2-10 years), Neutrophils 84%, Lymphocytes 15%. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: crackles over right lung middle zone
why_right: Five days of fever and cough with focal decreased air entry and crackles over the right middle zone, plus WBC 22 with 84% neutrophils, is bacterial pneumonia needing antibiotics. The child is stable: saturation 97%, normal blood pressure, no respiratory distress, so this is mild pneumonia managed at home with oral amoxicillin for 7 days.
why_wrong_block:
A. Reassurance alone ignores clear evidence of bacterial pneumonia (focal signs, neutrophilic leukocytosis) that needs antibiotics. Right for a simple viral URTI with a clear chest.
B. Bronchodilators and steroids treat wheeze from asthma or reactive airway disease; they do nothing for focal bacterial consolidation. Right if the child had diffuse wheeze and a known asthma picture.
C. IV antibiotics and admission are for severe or complicated pneumonia (hypoxaemia, distress, unable to drink, effusion). This child is stable with SpO2 97%.
key_concept:
Focal crackles + neutrophilic leukocytosis = bacterial pneumonia; severity decides the setting.
  • Mild and stable: oral amoxicillin at home
  • Severe: admit for IV antibiotics
  • Main pathogen at 3 months to 5 years: Streptococcus pneumoniae
exam_pearl: The diagnosis of pneumonia alone is not an admission criterion; look for hypoxaemia, distress or poor oral intake before choosing IV.

stem: 2 month old baby a product of 29 weeks (meaning he is premature) had been in the NICU and put off oxygen came to his vaccination appointment. He is healthy with a completely normal examination, his mother is worried about him acquiring bronchitis, what can you do for prevention?
OptD: Cough Is A Route Of Transmission
highlight_terms_source: healthy with a completely normal examination
key_concept:
How to decide RSV prophylaxis in a preterm infant:
  • Born before 29 weeks, first year of life: palivizumab
  • Chronic lung disease of prematurity or significant CHD: palivizumab
  • Born at 29 weeks or later, healthy, off oxygen: reassure + hygiene
  • Antibiotics have no preventive role
  • Current practice: long-acting nirsevimab is offered to all infants entering their first RSV season where available; the palivizumab criteria above are the classic exam rule
exam_pearl: The gestational age is the switch: 28 weeks favours palivizumab, 29 weeks and healthy favours reassurance with hygiene advice.

stem: Case for new born I forgot what he have but the ph low and hypokalemia? Urine pH 6.5
why_right: Low blood pH with hypokalaemia and a urine pH of 6.5 means the kidney cannot acidify the urine despite systemic acidosis. Inability to lower urine pH below 5.5 during acidosis is the defining feature of distal (type 1) RTA, where distal H+ secretion fails; it also wastes potassium.
why_wrong_block:
A. Proximal (type 2) RTA also causes hypokalaemia, but once serum bicarbonate falls the intact distal tubule can still acidify urine below 5.5. Right when urine pH is acidic during steady-state acidosis, or with Fanconi features.
B. There is no "medial" RTA; the recognised types are 1 (distal), 2 (proximal), 3 (rare mixed) and 4 (hyperkalaemic). This is a made-up distractor.
D. Fanconi syndrome is generalized proximal tubule failure (glycosuria with normal blood glucose, aminoaciduria, phosphaturia) causing a proximal RTA, so urine can still be acidified. Right when the stem lists those extra urinary losses or rickets.
key_concept:
All RTAs: non-anion-gap hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis. Separate by urine pH and potassium:
  • Type 1 (distal): urine pH > 5.5, low K, stones/nephrocalcinosis
  • Type 2 (proximal): urine pH < 5.5 once HCO3 is low, low K, Fanconi association
  • Type 4: urine pH < 5.5, HIGH K (aldosterone deficiency or resistance)
exam_pearl: Acidosis with an alkaline urine (pH > 5.5) = distal; if potassium is high instead of low, think type 4.

stem: Regarding febrile convulsions in children, which of the following statements is correct?
OptA: There is 2% chance to develop epilepsy
OptB: Anti epileptic medication daily will reduce the risk
OptC: Antipyretic during fever will reduce the risk of future epilepsy
OptD: The child will have intellectual disability
key_concept:
Febrile seizure: age about 6 months to 6 years with fever, benign prognosis.
  • Epilepsy risk after simple FS: about 1 to 2%
  • Higher with complex FS, abnormal development, family history of epilepsy
  • Antipyretics: comfort only, no preventive effect
  • Daily antiepileptics: not recommended, no effect on later epilepsy
  • No long-term cognitive sequelae
exam_pearl: Any option claiming that antipyretics or daily drugs reduce future epilepsy, or that the child will have intellectual disability, is a myth.

stem: Regarding febrile convulsions in children, which of the following statements is correct?
OptA: There is a 2% chance to develop epilepsy
OptB: If it is a complex febrile seizure, it is more likely to progress to epilepsy
OptC: If parents had febrile seizures, it will increase the chance to progress to epilepsy
OptD: Using antipyretics will decrease the chance of febrile convulsions
why_right: Febrile seizures are generally benign, but the risk of later epilepsy rises when the seizure is complex (focal, longer than 15 minutes, or recurring within 24 hours). Complex features are one of the main risk factors for epilepsy, along with abnormal neurodevelopment and a family history of epilepsy, so B is the reliably true statement.
why_wrong_block:
A. A risk of about 1 to 2% applies only to simple febrile seizures; stated as a fixed figure for all febrile seizures it ignores the higher risk with complex seizures, so it is weaker than B.
C. A parental history of febrile seizures raises the chance of the child having febrile seizures and recurrences, not epilepsy. It is a family history of EPILEPSY that increases the epilepsy risk.
D. Antipyretics make the child comfortable but have not been shown to prevent febrile convulsions or their recurrence.
key_concept:
Simple vs complex febrile seizure:
  • Simple: generalized, under 15 minutes, once in 24 hours
  • Complex: focal, over 15 minutes, or repeated within 24 hours
  • Epilepsy risk factors: complex FS, abnormal development, family history of epilepsy
  • Recurrence risk factors: young age at first seizure, family history of febrile seizures, low fever at seizure
exam_pearl: Family history of febrile seizures predicts recurrence; family history of epilepsy predicts epilepsy. Do not swap them.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0368).

stem: Newborn of diabetic mother with jittery movements. Asked About Management:
why_right: An infant of a diabetic mother has fetal hyperinsulinism that persists after birth, so glucose falls quickly. Jittery movements make this symptomatic hypoglycaemia until proven otherwise: check a bedside glucose and give IV dextrose (a 2 mL/kg 10% dextrose bolus followed by a continuous infusion). Symptomatic neonatal hypoglycaemia is treated intravenously, not with feeding or waiting.
why_wrong_block:
A. IM glucagon is a temporary rescue when IV access cannot be obtained; it is not the first-line treatment when IV dextrose can be given.
B. Feeding is appropriate for an asymptomatic or mildly low glucose. Once the baby is symptomatic (jittery), oral feeding is too slow and unreliable.
C. Waiting delays treatment of symptomatic hypoglycaemia and risks seizures and permanent brain injury.
key_concept:
Neonatal hypoglycaemia ladder:
  • At risk, asymptomatic: early feeding and glucose monitoring
  • Symptomatic (jittery, lethargy, poor feeding, seizure): IV 10% dextrose 2 mL/kg bolus then infusion
  • Peripheral line limit 12.5% dextrose; higher needs central access
  • No IV access: IM glucagon as a bridge
exam_pearl: Jitteriness in an infant of a diabetic mother is hypoglycaemia first; if glucose is normal, then check calcium (and consider polycythaemia).
compiler_note: Compiler note: Option notes by compiler: A IM glucagon, if after 72 hours we think hypocalcemia; B oral breast feeding, no benefit; C waiting 2 hours (not sure), no benefit. Infant of diabetic mother + jittery = symptomatic hypoglycemia = IV dextrose immediately; we should check blood sugar. Maternal hyperglycemia crosses placenta, fetal hyperinsulinemia persists after birth causing rapid hypoglycemia; jitteriness, tremors, lethargy, poor feeding, seizures are symptoms. Any jittery newborn = hypoglycemia until proven otherwise; if symptomatic do not wait or rely on feeding: IV dextrose ✅ bolus D10W 2 mL/kg then continuous infusion. Oral breastfeeding only for asymptomatic/mild hypoglycemia. Waiting 2 hours is dangerous: brain injury, seizures, permanent neurologic damage.

stem: A 3-day-old full-term infant presents with episodes of jitteriness and brief seizures lasting a few seconds that resolve spontaneously. Laboratory results are reported as normal; however, the glucose level was not provided. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
key_concept:
Neonatal seizure approach:
  • First: bedside glucose; correct hypoglycaemia with IV dextrose
  • Then: calcium, magnesium, sodium; sepsis work-up as indicated
  • Persistent seizures with metabolic causes corrected: phenobarbital first line
  • Jitteriness stops with gentle restraint; seizures do not
exam_pearl: When a stem says labs are normal but glucose was not given, the missing glucose is the point: check it and treat it first.

stem: Transient Tachypnea of the Newborn TTN pedia patient he was started on O2 and but still has mild respiratory distress. O2 sat 96%. How to feed.. RR is 65 ?
OptD: IV fluids and avoid oral feeding
highlight_terms_source: Transient Tachypnea of the Newborn TTN
why_right: TTN is a self limiting failure to clear fetal lung fluid, so the baby only needs support until it resolves. With a RR of 65 and mild distress despite O2, oral feeding is unsafe because the tachypneic infant cannot coordinate suck, swallow and breathe and may aspirate. The gut is normal, so enteral feeding should continue: nasogastric (gavage) feeds of expressed breast milk give nutrition without aspiration risk.
why_wrong_block:
B. Oral expressed breast milk: right milk, wrong route. Oral feeding is resumed once the respiratory rate settles and the baby can feed without distress; at RR 65 it risks aspiration.
C. TPN: reserved for babies who cannot use the gut for a prolonged period (e.g. extreme prematurity, NEC, gut failure). TTN resolves within days and the gut works.
D. IV fluids and nil by mouth: chosen when distress is severe (marked tachypnea, rising O2 need, impending ventilation). This baby has only mild distress with SpO2 96%, so enteral NGT feeds are preferred.
key_concept:
Feeding a tachypneic newborn scales with the severity of distress.
  • Mild tachypnea, feeding comfortably: oral / breastfeed
  • Moderate tachypnea or mild distress: NGT (gavage) feeds
  • Severe distress, high O2 need or ventilation: NPO + IV fluids
  • TTN: term, C-section, fluid in fissures on CXR, resolves in days
  • RDS: preterm, surfactant deficiency, ground glass CXR
exam_pearl: Persistent tachypnea with mild distress means bypass the mouth (NGT), not the gut; save NPO + IV for severe distress.

stem: A 3-year-old his mother is concerned that he does not interact or play with other children and prefers to play alone. The boy can speak [3- To 4 word Phrases (Literally Written Like This) ], jump, walk on his toes, run draw a rough circle, can’t draw figures,pour water into a cup, and follow complex commands. What is the most likely assessment of his development?
highlight_terms_source: does not interact or play with other children
why_right: Check each domain against age 3. Gross motor (jumps, runs), fine motor (rough circle, pours water) and language (3 to 4 word phrases, follows complex commands) are all on track. The only abnormal domain is social: he does not interact or play with other children and prefers to play alone, whereas a 3-year-old should be playing interactively with peers. An isolated social interaction deficit points to a psychosocial / social communication disorder that warrants autism screening.
why_wrong_block:
A. Gross motor delay: he jumps, runs and walks normally, which is age appropriate. Would apply if a 3-year-old could not climb stairs or run.
C. Normal development: motor and language are normal, but avoiding peer play at 3 years is not; a 3-year-old should have moved beyond solitary play.
D. Fine motor delay: drawing a rough circle and pouring water are appropriate; drawing a person or a square comes later (4 to 5 years), so being unable to draw figures is expected.
key_concept:
Assess development domain by domain; the abnormal domain names the answer.
  • 3 y gross motor: alternates feet on stairs, jumps, tricycle
  • 3 y fine motor: tower of 8 blocks, circle
  • 3 y language: 3 word sentences, 75% intelligible to strangers
  • Square at 5 y, person with 3 parts at 4 y
  • Social: pretend play at 2 y, interactive play with peers by 3 y
  • Isolated social deficit with normal motor and language: screen for autism
exam_pearl: Normal motor and speech do not make development normal; a 3-year-old who will not play with peers has a social domain problem.

stem: A 9-year-old boy who has nighttime enuresis 3 times a week and has never been dry . His urine CX and analysis are normal, and his PE is unremarkable. What should he do next?
why_right: A 9-year-old who has never been dry has primary nocturnal enuresis; normal urinalysis and culture and an unremarkable exam make it monosymptomatic with no organic cause. At this age it is no longer something to just wait out, so first line treatment is behavioural: limiting evening fluids, voiding before bed, a reward chart and an enuresis alarm (desmopressin is the drug alternative).
why_wrong_block:
A. MRI lumbar spine: only when there is a lumbosacral deformity, abnormal neurological exam or daytime symptoms with constipation suggesting a spinal defect; his exam is normal.
B. Referral to urology: needed for daytime symptoms, recurrent UTI (renal US and VCUG) or failure of first line therapy, not for uncomplicated monosymptomatic enuresis.
D. Reassure: appropriate in a younger child (under about 5 to 6 years), when bedwetting is still developmentally normal. At 9 years with frequent wetting, treatment is offered.
key_concept:
Nocturnal enuresis work up: UA for all, then classify.
  • Primary (never dry) vs secondary (dry, then relapse: look for stress, UTI, DM)
  • Normal UA + no daytime symptoms: monosymptomatic, treat with behavioural measures / alarm
  • Desmopressin: alternative or for short term needs
  • Recurrent UTI: renal US + VCUG
  • Spine deformity or abnormal neuro exam: MRI spine
  • Young child: reassure
exam_pearl: Age flips the answer: reassure the young child; treat with behavioural therapy / alarm once school aged.

stem: A 12-year-old boy is brought by his mother because she is concerned he might have contracted chickenpox after close contact with a child with chickenpox 2 days ago. What is the most appropriate next step?
highlight_terms_source: close contact with a child with chickenpox 2 days ago
why_right: Post exposure prophylaxis depends on immune status. This is a healthy 12-year-old exposed 2 days ago, with no vaccination or past chickenpox mentioned, so he is treated as non immune (unknown status). For an immunocompetent contact who is unvaccinated or of unknown status, varicella vaccine given early after exposure (ideally within 3 to 5 days) can prevent or modify the illness and also gives lasting immunity.
why_wrong_block:
A. Acyclovir: treats established varicella (IV in immunocompromised or high risk patients); it is not the first line prophylaxis for a healthy exposed child when the vaccine can be given.
B. IVIG (varicella zoster immunoglobulin): for exposed people who cannot receive a live vaccine, such as immunocompromised children, pregnant women without immunity and certain newborns.
D. Observe: correct if the child is already immune (vaccinated or past infection). Here immunity is not established, so prophylaxis is due.
key_concept:
Varicella post exposure prophylaxis by immune status.
  • Immunocompetent, vaccinated / immune: observe
  • Immunocompetent, unvaccinated or unknown: varicella vaccine (early after exposure)
  • Immunocompromised, asymptomatic: VZIG
  • Immunocompromised, symptomatic: IV acyclovir
  • Pregnant without immunity: VZIG (live vaccine contraindicated)
exam_pearl: Same exposure, different host: healthy child gets vaccine; leukemia on chemo gets VZIG.

stem: A 5 year old boy known case of leukemia, on chemotherapy and steroids for 6 weeks, presented to the clinic with his parents as he had contact with a child who has chickenpox, What to do?
highlight_terms_source: contact with a child who has chickenpox
why_right: This child is immunocompromised (leukemia on chemotherapy and steroids) and is a contact with no symptoms yet. He is at high risk of severe disseminated varicella, and a live vaccine is contraindicated, so passive immunisation with varicella zoster immunoglobulin is given as soon as possible after exposure.
why_wrong_block:
B. Admit and give acyclovir: IV acyclovir is for an immunocompromised child who has already developed varicella (symptomatic); he is only an asymptomatic contact.
C. Chickenpox vaccine: live attenuated, so contraindicated during chemotherapy and high dose steroids; it is the answer only for a healthy, non immune contact.
D. Stop chemotherapy: not part of post exposure management; interrupting leukemia treatment adds risk and does not prevent infection.
key_concept:
Varicella exposure: decide by host, then by symptoms.
  • Healthy, immune: observe
  • Healthy, non immune: vaccine
  • Immunocompromised, asymptomatic: VZIG
  • Immunocompromised, symptomatic: admit + IV acyclovir
  • Live vaccines (varicella, MMR) contraindicated on chemotherapy / high dose steroids
exam_pearl: Exposure without symptoms in an immunocompromised child = immunoglobulin; rash or symptoms = IV acyclovir.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Q: recall inside the 68 block; immunocompromised variant with a different answer from 68.

stem: A 8 months old baby, exclusively breastfeeding came with reduction in weight at birth he was 50th percentile now after month she is at 10th percentile, his height and head circumference still in 50th percentile.
highlight_terms_source: height and head circumference still in 50th percentile
why_right: Weight has fallen from the 50th to the 10th percentile, crossing two major centile lines, while length and head circumference stay on the 50th. A weight only drop with preserved growth of length and head points to inadequate caloric intake rather than an organic disease. At 8 months breast milk alone no longer meets energy needs (complementary foods should start around 6 months), so the advice is to increase calorie intake.
why_wrong_block:
A. Metabolic disorder: suspected when growth failure is global (length and head also falling) or with vomiting, lethargy, acidosis or developmental regression; here only weight is affected and the infant is otherwise well.
C. Reassure: crossing two major percentile lines is not a normal fluctuation and needs action; reassurance fits physiological early weight loss or small shifts within a centile channel.
key_concept:
Pattern of growth failure points to the cause.
  • Weight falls first, length and head preserved: inadequate intake (nutritional)
  • Weight and length both down, head preserved: endocrine or genetic short stature
  • All three down including head: congenital, genetic or CNS cause
  • Exclusive breastfeeding to about 6 months, then add complementary foods
  • Weight gain slows to about 10 to 15 g/day at 6 to 12 months
exam_pearl: Exclusively breastfed past 6 months with weight only centile drop: the fix is more calories (start solids), not a metabolic work up.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Alternate recall (Q:): 8 month old exclusively breastfeeding, weight 50th then 10th percentile, parent worried, advice to prevent further decline: A Improve caloric intake (highlighted), B Weight fluctuation is normal at this age, C metabolic screening, D Reassurance.

stem: A 4 months old baby, exclusively breastfeeding came with reduction in weight at birth he was 50th percentile now after month she is at 10th percentile, his height and head circumference still in 50th percentile. Her parent is worried, What advice to give the parent to prevent further decline in weight?
key_concept:
Weight only centile fall with preserved length and head suggests a nutritional cause.
  • Crossing ≥2 major centile lines: abnormal, needs action
  • Weight down, length and head preserved: inadequate intake
  • Head and length also down: think organic, genetic, CNS
  • Exclusive breastfeeding is appropriate until about 6 months
  • Expected gain 3 to 6 months: about 20 g/day
exam_pearl: Decide how far the weight has dropped: one channel can be reassured, two major lines with spared length and head means feeding is inadequate.
