stem: A 3-month-old infant with noisy breath since birth change with positioning; disappears in prone position and become more obvious with supine position. Examination and growth parameter are normal. The mother concerned about this sound. Which of the following is the most appropriate counselling should be given?
OptD: Will improve by her first birthday
highlight_terms_source: disappears in prone position and become more obvious with supine position
Examination and growth parameter are normal
why_right: Noisy breathing since birth that disappears prone and is worse supine with normal growth and examination is laryngomalacia: floppy supraglottic tissue collapses on inspiration. It is self-limiting and usually resolves by 1 to 2 years, so the correct counselling is reassurance that it will improve by her first birthday.
why_wrong_block:
A. Will worsen with time: the noise may peak in the first months but laryngomalacia does not progressively worsen; it improves as the airway matures.
B. Needs surgical correction: supraglottoplasty is reserved for severe disease with failure to thrive, apnea, cyanosis or feeding difficulty; this infant is thriving.
C. Normal developmental sounds: the noise comes from a structural airway disorder (laryngomalacia), even though it is benign; calling it normal skips the diagnosis and the expected course.
key_concept:
Congenital stridor by position:
  • Better prone, worse supine = laryngomalacia (diagnosis: laryngoscopy)
  • Better supine = tracheomalacia (diagnosis: bronchoscopy)
  • Both self-limiting, resolve by 1 to 2 years
  • Red flags for surgery: failure to thrive, apnea, cyanosis, feeding problems
exam_pearl: Thriving infant with positional stridor: reassure; the answer flips to surgery only if growth falters or there are apneas or cyanosis.

stem: Meconium aspiration with severe respiratory distress. What to do?
why_right: Meconium aspiration with severe respiratory distress means respiratory failure: meconium blocks airways, inactivates surfactant and causes chemical pneumonitis and often pulmonary hypertension. A neonate in severe distress cannot be supported by supplemental oxygen alone, so the next step is to secure the airway with intubation and provide mechanical ventilation (with surfactant and treatment of pulmonary hypertension as needed).
why_wrong_block:
A. Mask oxygen: fits mild distress with adequate effort; it does not support ventilation or provide pressure in severe distress.
C. Low-flow oxygen: suitable only for mild hypoxemia without significant distress; it is inadequate for a neonate in respiratory failure.
key_concept:
Meconium aspiration syndrome:
  • Risk: post-term, fetal distress, meconium-stained liquor
  • Vigorous baby: routine care, no tracheal suctioning
  • Non-vigorous baby: start resuscitation with PPV; routine tracheal suctioning is no longer recommended
  • Severe distress or respiratory failure: intubation and mechanical ventilation, surfactant, treat pulmonary hypertension (inhaled nitric oxide, ECMO if refractory)
  • CXR: patchy infiltrates with hyperinflation
exam_pearl: Severity decides support: mild distress gets oxygen, severe distress gets intubation and ventilation.

stem: A 2-month-old baby (chronological age) born at 34 weeks gestation. Mother presents to the clinic for immunization.
why_right: A 34 week baby who is now 2 months chronological age gets the standard 2-month vaccines today. Preterm infants are immunized according to chronological age with full doses, because their immune response at that age is adequate and delaying leaves them unprotected when they are most vulnerable.
why_wrong_block:
B. Prematurity schedule (corrected age): corrected age is used for growth and developmental assessment, not vaccine timing; there is no separate delayed schedule for preterm infants.
C. Immunize for 6 months: giving the 6-month vaccines now would be too early and skips the 2 and 4 month doses; the schedule follows actual age.
key_concept:
Preterm vaccination rule:
  • Timing: chronological age
  • Dose: full dose, never reduced
  • Corrected age: growth and development only (until about 2 years)
  • Exception: hepatitis B birth dose in infants under 2 kg depends on maternal HBsAg status
exam_pearl: Vaccines follow chronological age; milestones and growth follow corrected age.

stem: Child fell down then had tonic-clonic seizure, came to the ER, drowsy but rousable, neurological exam is normal (includes pupils etc.). Best step:
why_right: A child who "fell" and then had a tonic-clonic seizure and is now "drowsy but rousable" has two high-risk features after head trauma: a post-traumatic seizure and altered mental status (drowsiness counts even with a normal focal exam). These place the child in the group needing urgent non-contrast head CT to exclude an intracranial bleed. Non-contrast CT is the fastest test to show acute blood, and a normal pupil and limb exam does not exclude a hematoma.
why_wrong_block: B. Admit for observation 24 hours: observation alone suits a child with minor head injury, normal mental status and only intermediate features (brief vomiting, headache, no LOC). A post-traumatic seizure with drowsiness needs imaging first; observation follows a normal CT.
key_concept:
Pediatric head trauma: image when high-risk features are present, observe when only intermediate features exist.
  • CT now: altered mental status or GCS <15, post-traumatic seizure, signs of skull base or depressed fracture, focal deficit
  • Observation vs CT: brief LOC, vomiting, severe headache, severe mechanism, with normal mental status
  • Neither: minor mechanism, normal child
  • CT is non-contrast (blood is bright on plain CT); MRI is not first-line acutely
exam_pearl: A normal neuro exam does not cancel CT if the child seized after the fall or is drowsy; those features alone mandate imaging.

stem: Bronchiolitis typical symptoms. Next step?
OptA: High flow O2 and IV fluids
OptB: Low flow O2, supportive care, suction
why_right: Bronchiolitis (usually RSV) is a self-limiting viral illness with no curative drug, so management is supportive: oxygen if saturation is low, nasal suctioning to clear the airway (infants are obligate nose breathers), and maintaining hydration and feeding. For a "typical" case without signs of severe distress or fatigue, low flow oxygen is the right level of support.
why_wrong_block: A. High flow O2 and IV fluids: an escalation step for severe disease (marked work of breathing, persistent hypoxia on low flow, apnea, or inability to feed). Not the starting point for a typical case.
key_concept:
Bronchiolitis = clinical diagnosis; treatment = oxygen + hydration + suction, escalated by severity.
  • Mild: home, nasal suction, small frequent feeds
  • Moderate (hypoxia, tachypnea, poor feeding): admit, low flow O2, NG or IV fluids if not feeding
  • Severe/failing: high flow, CPAP/NIV in PICU
  • Not routinely used: bronchodilators, steroids, antibiotics, routine CXR
exam_pearl: Apnea in a young infant or rising work of breathing despite low flow oxygen flips management to high flow/NIV and critical care.

stem: Child with sore throat for 2 days. Exam: enlarged tonsils with exudate, pharyngeal petechiae, anterior and posterior cervical lymphadenopathy. Rapid strep positive. T = 39°C. Others normal. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: Fever of 39°C, tonsillar exudate and cervical nodes with a "rapid strep positive" result confirms group A streptococcal pharyngitis; no further test is needed. The next step is antibiotic treatment, and oral penicillin V for a full 10-day course is first line (amoxicillin is an accepted equivalent). The full course is what prevents acute rheumatic fever.
why_wrong_block:
B. Throat culture: the back-up test when the rapid antigen test is NEGATIVE in a child with a suggestive picture. A positive rapid test is specific enough to treat without culture.
C. Reassurance: appropriate for viral pharyngitis (mild hyperemia, negative rapid test). Confirmed GAS needs antibiotics to prevent rheumatic fever and suppurative complications.
D. This option was blank in the recall and carries no content.
key_concept:
Sore throat in a child: test before treating, treat only confirmed GAS.
  • Suggestive picture: rapid antigen detection test first
  • RADT positive: treat (penicillin V or amoxicillin, 10 days)
  • RADT negative in a child: confirm with throat culture
  • Penicillin allergy: macrolide or cephalosporin by allergy type
  • Asymptomatic contacts: observe, no prophylaxis
exam_pearl: Exudate with posterior cervical nodes also fits EBV mononucleosis; the positive rapid strep settles it as GAS here, but if EBV is likely, amoxicillin often provokes a widespread rash.

stem: A 6-year-old child seen at pre-school screening clinic. What are the recommended vaccines at this stage according to national program in Saudi Arabia?
why_right: At pre-school / primary school entry the Saudi national schedule gives the booster set: OPV, DTaP, MMR and varicella. This is exactly option C. The "6-year-old" at school screening is the cue for the school-entry visit.
why_wrong_block:
A. MMR.DTP.OPV: incomplete; it leaves out varicella, which is also given at school entry.
B. MMR.HBV.DTP.HAV: hepatitis B is completed in infancy and hepatitis A at 18 and 24 months, so neither belongs at school entry; varicella and OPV are missing.
D. MMR.varicella.OPV.PCV: PCV is an infant series vaccine (2, 4, 6, 12 months) and is not routine in a healthy 6-year-old; DTP is missing.
key_concept:
Saudi schedule anchor visits:
  • Birth: BCG, Hep B
  • 2, 4 months: IPV, DTaP, Hep B, Hib, PCV, rotavirus
  • 6 months: OPV, IPV, DTaP, Hep B, Hib, PCV
  • 9 months: measles, MCV4; 12 months: OPV, MMR, PCV, MCV4
  • 18 months: OPV, DTaP, Hib, MMR, varicella, Hep A; 24 months: Hep A
  • School entry: OPV, DTaP, MMR, varicella
exam_pearl: School entry repeats the 18-month boosters minus Hib and Hep A: OPV, DTaP, MMR, varicella.

stem: Name of the reflex? (in the picture)
why_right: The picture shows a finger stroking the newborn's cheek with the mouth opening and turning toward it. Turning the head and mouth toward a touch at the side of the mouth is the rooting reflex, present from birth and fading by about 4 months.
why_wrong_block: B. Suckling: the sucking reflex is triggered by something placed INSIDE the mouth or touching the palate, producing rhythmic sucking; stroking the cheek causes rooting, not sucking.

Mouth reflexes of the newborn:
  • Rooting: stroke cheek or corner of mouth, head turns and mouth opens toward stimulus; gone by about 4 months
  • Sucking: object in mouth or on palate, rhythmic sucking
  • Both help feeding; absence suggests CNS depression
exam_pearl: Cheek touched = rooting; object in the mouth = sucking.

stem: 6-Year-Old Bedwetting, Never Been Dry At Night, His Brother Had The Same Problem. Next Step?
why_right: A 6-year-old who has never been dry at night has primary nocturnal enuresis, and a sibling with the same problem shows the strong familial tendency. At this age bedwetting is still common and resolves spontaneously in most children each year, so the first step is reassurance with simple behavioural advice (no punishment, voiding before bed, limiting evening fluids).
why_wrong_block:
B. Desmopressin is for older children when behavioural measures and the alarm fail, or for short-term needs such as sleepovers; it is not the first step at 6.
C. Toilet training addresses daytime continence, which is usually already achieved; nighttime dryness depends on bladder maturation and ADH rhythm, not training.
D. The enuresis alarm is the most effective active treatment once a motivated older child and family want treatment after behavioural measures; it is not the first step here.
key_concept:
Primary nocturnal enuresis:
  • Bedwetting is considered significant after about 6 years
  • Strong family history; spontaneous resolution each year
  • Ladder: reassurance and behavioural measures → enuresis alarm → desmopressin (oral, not intranasal)
  • Secondary enuresis (previously dry) or daytime symptoms: look for UTI, diabetes, constipation, stress
exam_pearl: Never dry + family history + young age = reassure; new bedwetting after being dry = investigate (urinalysis, glucose).

stem: A 3-year-old child Play Alone, obeys complex commands, pours water from a pitcher, but cannot draw a circle. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
why_right: At 3 years the child "obeys complex commands" (receptive language on track) and "pours water from a pitcher" (good fine motor and self-help control). In the milestone table used for this exam, copying a circle is a 4-year skill, so not drawing one yet is not a delay, and playing alone (solitary or parallel play) is still common at this age. With no domain clearly behind and no gross motor problem described, the profile is read as normal for age.
why_wrong_block:
B. Psychosocial development delay: would need clear social red flags (no interest in peers, no pretend play, poor eye contact, loss of skills). "Plays alone" by itself, with intact comprehension, is not enough.
C. Gross motor delay: no gross motor finding is given (walking, running, stairs, tricycle); pouring water and drawing are fine motor tasks.
D. This option was not recalled ("Forget") and carries no content.
key_concept:
Judge development by domain, and call delay only when a domain misses its expected age.
  • 3 years: stairs with alternating feet, tricycle, 3-word sentences, speech 75% intelligible, uses spoon well, parallel play moving to group play
  • 4 years: hops on one foot, copies a circle (per this table), draws person with 3 parts, tells stories
  • 5 years: copies a square; 6 years: copies a triangle
exam_pearl: Check which domain the missing skill belongs to: an isolated fine motor item with everything else normal does not make a gross motor or global delay.

stem: Pediatric girl with diabetes uncontrolled, her glucose was high. What to do? The stem was something education promotion preventive bla bla.
OptA: Teach family how to insulin use and diet basics
OptB: Give them pamphlet and arrange follow up
OptC: Refer him to somewhere I don't remember (in my exam)
why_right: Poor glycemic control in a child with diabetes is most often due to gaps in day-to-day self-management, and the stem frames the question as education / health promotion. The most effective step is direct, hands-on education of the family: insulin technique and dosing, glucose monitoring, diet basics, and recognizing and treating hypoglycemia. Active teaching with return demonstration changes behavior; passive measures do not.

B. Give them pamphlet and arrange follow up: written material alone is passive and does not check understanding or skill; it supplements but does not replace face-to-face teaching.

  • Teach insulin injection, dosing and site rotation
  • Glucose monitoring and sick-day rules
  • Diet basics (carbohydrate awareness, regular meals)
  • Hypoglycemia recognition and treatment (most important insulin adverse effect)
  • Involve the whole family and school

stem: Newborn reflex shown in images (infant held upright with feet touching surface, making stepping movements). Name of the reflex?
why_right: The images show the infant held upright with the feet touching a surface, making alternating step movements. This walking-like response is the stepping reflex, present at birth and normally fading in the first couple of months.

  • Dorsum of foot touches table edge: placing
  • Cheek stroked: rooting
  • Head turned supine, fencing posture: ATNR
  • Head drop: Moro
  • Held face down toward table, arms extend: parachute (appears 8 to 10 months)

stem: Newborn stepping reflex (shown in images). Time of disappearance?
why_right: The stepping (walking) reflex is present at birth and is one of the earliest primitive reflexes to fade, usually disappearing by about 2 months. That makes "by 2 months" the correct disappearance age.
why_wrong_block:
B. By 4 months: the typical disappearance age of the rooting and Galant (trunk incurvation) reflexes, not stepping.
C. By 6 months: the disappearance age of the Moro and palmar grasp reflexes.
key_concept:
Primitive reflex disappearance ages:
  • About 2 months: stepping; ATNR about 2 to 3 months
  • About 4 months: rooting, Galant; placing 4 to 6 months
  • About 6 months: Moro, palmar grasp
  • 12 to 18 months: Babinski
  • Parachute appears at 8 to 10 months and persists for life
exam_pearl: Reflexes that persist well beyond their expected age suggest CNS pathology such as cerebral palsy.

stem: A newborn is delivered with cleft palate, micrognathia, and glossoptosis. He has difficulty suckling and breathing, is partially fed via NG tube, and experiences random episodes of apnea. What is the most appropriate management?
OptA: Refer to ENT and continue NG tube feeding until ENT evaluation
OptB: Refer for sleep study and provide NG tube feeding for evaluation of breathing
OptC: Refer for palate surgery and respiratory monitoring
OptD: Counsel cardio and genetics while maintaining NGT for feeding
key_concept:
Pierre Robin sequence: micrognathia → glossoptosis → upper airway obstruction (often with cleft palate).
  • First: airway (prone or lateral positioning, nasopharyngeal airway, airway/ENT team)
  • Feeding: special cleft feeders or NG tube; monitor weight
  • Sleep study to grade obstruction once stable
  • Severe or refractory: mandibular distraction or tongue lip adhesion; tracheostomy rarely
  • Genetics: screen for Stickler, 22q11 deletion
  • Palate repair is delayed to later infancy
exam_pearl: Apnea in Pierre Robin is obstructive from the tongue, so the airway team comes before the palate surgeon.

stem: Pediatric boy presents with low-set ears, hypertelorism, webbed neck. On examination: pulmonary stenosis and came with history of failure to thrive. What is the most appropriate next step?
OptA: Refer to cardiology and genetic testing
OptB: Refer to endocrinology and measure growth hormone
why_right: A boy with "low-set ears, hypertelorism, webbed neck", pulmonary stenosis and failure to thrive has the classic picture of Noonan syndrome (a male phenotype resembling Turner, with normal karyotype). The next step is to evaluate the heart lesion with cardiology (echo; hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is also associated) and confirm the diagnosis with genetic testing (RASopathy gene panel).
why_wrong_block:
B. Short stature in Noonan can later be treated with growth hormone, but the priority now is the cardiac lesion and confirming the syndrome; endocrine referral first fits isolated short stature without dysmorphism or heart disease.
C. Gastroenterology referral fits failure to thrive with GI symptoms (malabsorption, chronic diarrhea); here the failure to thrive is part of a syndromic picture with a heart lesion.
key_concept:
Webbed neck + pulmonary stenosis in a boy = Noonan syndrome.
  • Noonan: autosomal dominant, normal karyotype, males and females; PS, HCM
  • Turner: girls only, 45,X; coarctation and bicuspid aortic valve
  • Next step: cardiology (echo) + genetic testing
  • Other features: short stature, pectus, cryptorchidism, bleeding tendency
exam_pearl: Turner features in a boy, or with pulmonary stenosis instead of coarctation, means Noonan.

stem: Pediatric came after a fall while playing, currently stable. ECG picture provided and was SVT. What is the treatment (not sure if it was initial or most appropriate)?
why_right: This recall's key is cardioversion: synchronized electrical cardioversion terminates SVT immediately and is the right choice when the child is hemodynamically unstable or when vagal maneuvers and adenosine fail. The stem, however, says the child is "currently stable", which normally points to vagal maneuvers then adenosine (see the concern note).
why_wrong_block:
A. Amiodarone is reserved for refractory SVT under cardiology guidance after adenosine and cardioversion are considered; it is not a first line drug in children.
B. Adenosine is the usual drug for stable SVT once vagal maneuvers (ice to face, Valsalva) fail; the key here skips it, which only fits a child who is unstable or adenosine refractory.
D. Beta blockers are used for long term prevention of recurrent SVT, not for acute termination of an ongoing episode.
key_concept:
Pediatric SVT ladder: check stability first.
  • Unstable (hypotension, poor perfusion, altered consciousness): synchronized cardioversion
  • Stable: vagal maneuvers (ice to face in infants, Valsalva in older children)
  • Then IV adenosine (rapid push with flush)
  • Refractory: cardioversion or expert-guided drugs
  • Long term prevention: beta blocker; ablation for recurrent cases
exam_pearl: The word "stable" flips the answer from cardioversion to vagal maneuvers then adenosine.

stem: A mother of a 2-month-old infant complains that her baby has frequent episodes of excessive crying, 3 hours, raises legs and passes gas. She asks how to treat?
why_right: A 2-month-old with crying bouts lasting about "3 hours", drawing up the legs and passing gas, with no red flags, has infantile colic. Colic is self limiting (usually settles by 3 to 4 months), so management is reassurance and behavioral soothing such as rhythmic motion, swaddling, holding and white noise.
why_wrong_block:
A. Simethicone is widely used but trials show no benefit over placebo, so it is not the recommended treatment.
C. Antibiotics would only fit an infection with fever, poor feeding or toxic appearance; colic is not infectious.
D. Abdominal ultrasound is for red flags such as bilious vomiting, abdominal mass, distension or bloody stools (for example intussusception); a thriving infant with colic needs no imaging.
key_concept:
Infantile colic, rule of 3s: crying >3 h/day, >3 days/week, >3 weeks in a healthy, thriving infant.
  • Onset around 2 weeks, peaks about 6 weeks, resolves by 3 to 4 months
  • Treatment: reassurance + soothing (motion, swaddling, white noise)
  • Support the parents; screen for exhaustion
  • Red flags (fever, vomiting, poor weight gain, blood in stool) need work up
exam_pearl: A thriving infant with evening crying and leg drawing needs reassurance and soothing, not drops or tests.

stem: Child brought by his mother with diarrhoea; the mother noted that there is blood and mucus. Most likely cause?
why_right: "Blood and mucus" in the stool means dysentery (inflammatory, invasive diarrhea), which is bacterial rather than viral. Among the listed options only Campylobacter is an invasive bacterium, and it is one of the commonest causes of bloody diarrhea in children.
why_wrong_block:
A. Rotavirus causes watery, non bloody diarrhea with vomiting and fever in infants and young children; it is the classic cause of dehydrating watery diarrhea.
B. Norovirus causes acute vomiting and watery diarrhea, typically in outbreaks (schools, cruise ships); no blood or mucus.
C. This option was not recalled; other causes of bloody mucoid diarrhea a student should consider are Shigella (especially with high fever or seizures), Salmonella, EHEC (bloody diarrhea then HUS) and amebiasis.
key_concept:
Stool character sorts the cause.
  • Watery: viral (rotavirus, norovirus, adenovirus), ETEC, cholera
  • Blood + mucus (dysentery): Campylobacter, Shigella, Salmonella, EHEC, Entamoeba
  • Bloody diarrhea + seizures: Shigella
  • Bloody diarrhea then renal failure: EHEC O157 → HUS
  • Campylobacter: linked to undercooked poultry; Guillain-Barré later
exam_pearl: Blood and mucus means bacterial; if seizures are added, choose Shigella.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Blood and mucus in diarrhea usually indicates inflammatory (invasive) diarrhea, most commonly bacterial, not viral. Campylobacter causes inflammatory diarrhea with blood and mucus, abdominal pain, sometimes fever; one of the most common bacterial causes of dysentery in children. Watery diarrhea = viral (Rotavirus, Norovirus); bloody + mucus (dysentery) = bacterial (Campylobacter, Shigella, EHEC). Refs: Nelson; CDC.

stem: Regarding febrile convulsions in children, which of the following statements is correct?
OptA: There is a 2% chance to develop epilepsy
OptB: If it is a complex febrile seizure, it is more likely to progress to epilepsy
OptC: If parents had febrile seizures, it will increase the chance to progress to epilepsy
OptD: Using antipyretics will decrease the chance of febrile convulsions
why_right: Febrile seizures are generally benign, but the risk of later epilepsy rises when the seizure is complex (focal, longer than 15 minutes, or recurring within 24 hours). Complex features are one of the main risk factors for epilepsy, along with abnormal neurodevelopment and a family history of epilepsy, so B is the reliably true statement.
why_wrong_block:
A. A risk of about 1 to 2% applies only to simple febrile seizures; stated as a fixed figure for all febrile seizures it ignores the higher risk with complex seizures, so it is weaker than B.
C. A parental history of febrile seizures raises the chance of the child having febrile seizures and recurrences, not epilepsy. It is a family history of EPILEPSY that increases the epilepsy risk.
D. Antipyretics make the child comfortable but have not been shown to prevent febrile convulsions or their recurrence.
key_concept:
Simple vs complex febrile seizure:
  • Simple: generalized, under 15 minutes, once in 24 hours
  • Complex: focal, over 15 minutes, or repeated within 24 hours
  • Epilepsy risk factors: complex FS, abnormal development, family history of epilepsy
  • Recurrence risk factors: young age at first seizure, family history of febrile seizures, low fever at seizure
exam_pearl: Family history of febrile seizures predicts recurrence; family history of epilepsy predicts epilepsy. Do not swap them.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0038).

stem: A newborn presents with persistent bleeding after circumcision that does not stop with compression. There is a positive family history of a bleeding disorder affecting both his brother and mother (no labs). What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: Bleeding is inherited in a pattern that affects both sexes: the "brother and mother" are both affected. That fits an autosomal dominant disorder, and von Willebrand disease (commonest inherited bleeding disorder, usually autosomal dominant) explains a symptomatic mother, whereas hemophilia carrier mothers are usually not affected.
why_wrong_block:
A. Hemophilia A is X linked recessive: it affects boys and is classic for post circumcision bleeding, but the mother is usually an asymptomatic carrier; choose it when only male relatives (brothers, maternal uncles) bleed.
C. DIC is acquired, occurring in a sick neonate (sepsis, asphyxia) with diffuse bleeding; a family history makes no sense for it.
D. Inherited platelet disorders (for example Glanzmann, Bernard-Soulier) are rare and usually autosomal recessive; they need platelet count and function tests, and are less likely than vWD with this pattern.
key_concept:
Use the family pattern to choose the bleeding disorder.
  • Only males affected, mother a carrier: hemophilia A or B (X linked)
  • Both sexes affected (mother + son): von Willebrand disease (AD)
  • vWD: mucosal bleeding, prolonged bleeding time/PFA, ± prolonged aPTT (low factor VIII)
  • Hemophilia: prolonged aPTT only, joint and muscle bleeds
  • DIC: acquired, low platelets and fibrinogen, prolonged PT and aPTT
exam_pearl: An affected mother points to vWD; an unaffected carrier mother with affected sons points to hemophilia.
compiler_note:
⚠ The same question appears elsewhere in this file with a DIFFERENT marked answer: AS-0602 → A. Hemophilia A. Confirm before the exam.
Compiler note: Answer: B ✅. Details: NCBI Bookshelf NBK459222.

stem: 14 year old boy came in for pre-sport screening; he had a murmur, his dad died at 40 years old. ECG shows long QT:
OptA: Continue sport and do annual ECG
OptB: Give beta blocker and only do sports that require low effort
OptC: Don't do sport and consider pacemaker
why_right: A teenager with a long QT on ECG and a father who died suddenly at 40 most likely has congenital long QT syndrome, a cause of sudden cardiac death during exertion. Management is a beta blocker (first line, reduces arrhythmic events) and avoiding competitive or strenuous sports, allowing only low intensity activity.
why_wrong_block:
A. Continuing sports with only annual ECGs leaves an untreated, high risk patient exposed to exertion triggered arrhythmia; it fits only a normal screening ECG.
C. Pacemaker is not first line; it is considered for bradycardia or pause dependent torsades, and an ICD (not a pacemaker) is for survivors of cardiac arrest or recurrent events despite beta blockers.
D. Unrestricted sport would be correct only after the abnormal ECG and family history are explained and excluded; a long QT with family sudden death is not cleared.
key_concept:
Congenital long QT: beta blocker + restrict strenuous sport.
  • Triggers: exercise and swimming (LQT1), loud noise or startle (LQT2), sleep (LQT3)
  • First line: beta blocker (propranolol or nadolol)
  • Avoid QT prolonging drugs; correct K and Mg
  • ICD: aborted arrest or events despite beta blocker
  • Screen first degree relatives with ECG
exam_pearl: Pacemaker is a distractor; the device for high risk long QT is an ICD, and only after beta blockers.

stem: 14 year old boy came in for pre-sport screening; he had a murmur, his dad died at 40 years old. ECG shows long QT?
OptA: Continue sport and do annual ECG
OptB: Restrict sport and give beta blocker
OptC: Do minimal sport and consider pacemaker
OptD: Only do sport with low exertion
why_right: A long QT on ECG with a father who died suddenly at 40 suggests congenital long QT syndrome, in which exertion can trigger fatal arrhythmia. The standard answer is to start a beta blocker and restrict competitive or strenuous sport, covering both treatment and the trigger.
why_wrong_block:
A. Continuing sports with only annual ECG monitoring ignores a high risk diagnosis; this fits only a normal screening ECG.
C. Pacemaker is not first line in long QT; an ICD is reserved for aborted cardiac arrest or recurrent events despite beta blockers.
D. Limiting to low exertion sport addresses the trigger but gives no beta blocker, which is the cornerstone of therapy; the combined option is better.
key_concept:
Congenital long QT: beta blocker + restrict strenuous sport.
  • First line: beta blocker (propranolol or nadolol)
  • Avoid QT prolonging drugs and electrolyte disturbance
  • ICD for aborted arrest or breakthrough events
  • ECG screening of first degree relatives
exam_pearl: When one option gives activity advice alone and another adds a beta blocker, choose the one with the beta blocker.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer written at top of next page as 'B??' (tentative).

stem: 4 month-old infant has been at the 25th percentile for weight and length since birth. Development is normal, feeding is adequate, but the family is concerned about growth. What is the most appropriate next step?
OptA: Continue routine follow-up in well-baby clinic and keep up-to-date with vaccinations
OptB: Postpone follow-up and monitor weight weekly at home
OptC: Refer to endocrinology for growth hormone evaluation
OptD: Increase caloric intake to accelerate growth
highlight_terms_source: 25th percentile for weight and length since birth
why_right: The infant has stayed on the "25th percentile ... since birth" for both weight and length, with normal development and adequate feeding. Steady tracking along a percentile within the normal range is normal growth, so the right step is reassurance with routine well baby follow-up and vaccinations.
why_wrong_block:
B. Postponing clinic follow-up and weighing weekly at home is unnecessary and removes routine surveillance; weekly weights fit a baby with faltering growth.
C. Growth hormone evaluation is for falling height velocity or crossing length percentiles downward, often with low bone age; proportionate tracking on the 25th percentile is normal.
D. Extra calories are for failure to thrive (weight crossing percentiles downward); forcing calories in a normally growing infant risks overfeeding.
key_concept:
Growth charts: the trend matters more than the percentile.
  • Stable tracking on any normal percentile: normal, routine follow-up
  • Weight crossing percentile lines downward: assess for failure to thrive
  • Weight falls before length: nutritional cause
  • Length falls with weight preserved: endocrine cause
  • Proportionally small with short parents: familial short stature
exam_pearl: A low but stable percentile is reassuring; crossing percentile lines is what needs work up.

stem: 4 month old baby presents to the clinic for routine visit; she has consistent growth on 25th percentile for both weight and height since birth. She is feeding well and has normal development. Her parents are concerned about her being too small. What should you do?
OptA: Refer to endocrinologist for growth hormone assessment
why_right: The decisive clue is "consistent growth on 25th percentile for both weight and height since birth" with "feeding well" and "normal development". A child who tracks steadily along one percentile inside the normal range (5th to 95th) is growing normally; the 25th percentile simply reflects constitutional/genetic size. The correct action is to reassure the parents and keep plotting growth at routine visits.
why_wrong_block:
A. Growth hormone assessment is for true growth failure: height below the normal range or a falling height velocity (crossing percentiles downward). Steady tracking at the 25th percentile is not growth failure.
C. Increasing calories is for inadequate intake or weight faltering (weight crossing percentiles downward). Here feeding is good and weight and height are proportionate and stable.
D. Small size is never a reason to delay immunization; vaccines are given on schedule. Delay applies only to true contraindications or precautions (e.g., moderate to severe acute illness).
key_concept:
Growth charts: the pattern over time matters more than a single percentile.
  • Steady tracking on any percentile within 5th to 95th: normal, reassure and follow
  • Crossing percentiles downward (even within normal range): concern for failure to thrive, evaluate/refer
  • Moving upward across percentiles: improvement
  • Weight and height on the same percentile: proportionate, reassuring
exam_pearl: If the same baby had dropped from the 50th to the 25th percentile, the answer flips from reassurance to evaluation for failure to thrive.

stem: 9 month old baby exclusively breastfeeding. Weight is 10th percentile. What advice to give?
OptB: Weight fluctuation is normal at this age.
why_right: The key clue is a "9 month old" who is still "exclusively breastfeeding". Breast milk alone stops meeting an infant's energy and iron needs after about 6 months, which is why complementary foods are introduced at that age. A 9-month-old on breast milk only, with weight at the 10th percentile, needs advice to improve caloric intake by adding energy-dense complementary foods (while continuing breastfeeding).
why_wrong_block:
B. Day-to-day weight fluctuation is normal, but it does not address the real problem: a 9-month-old with no complementary feeding. Reassurance alone fits a well-fed infant tracking steadily on a percentile.
C. Adding protein alone is too narrow; the deficit at this age is overall energy (and iron) from missing complementary foods. A protein-specific change would fit only a documented protein deficiency, which is not suggested here.
key_concept:
Exclusive breastfeeding is recommended for about the first 6 months; then add complementary foods.
  • After 6 months, breast milk alone is insufficient in energy and iron
  • Delayed weaning: poor weight gain and iron deficiency anemia
  • Advice: introduce complementary (energy-dense, iron-rich) foods and continue breastfeeding
  • 6 to 12 months: expected weight gain slows, so watch the trend, not one value
exam_pearl: The trap is the word "exclusively" at 9 months: the problem is the feeding plan, not the percentile itself.

stem: 2 month old Down syndrome baby with poor feeding and interrupted feeding, hepatosplenomegaly, murmur, other symptoms. Management?
why_right: "Down syndrome" plus "poor feeding and interrupted feeding, hepatosplenomegaly, murmur" at 2 months describes heart failure from a large left to right shunt, most likely an atrioventricular septal defect (the commonest lesion in Down syndrome). A complete AVSD does not close spontaneously and causes early pulmonary vascular disease, especially in Down syndrome, so the definitive management is early surgical repair in infancy (around 3 to 6 months), with anti-failure medication only as a bridge.
why_wrong_block:
A. Diuretics and other heart failure drugs control symptoms until surgery but do not correct the defect; medical treatment alone fits a small, asymptomatic, or spontaneously closing defect (e.g., small muscular VSD).
B. Higher-calorie feeds support weight gain in a child with heart failure, but they are adjunctive and do not treat the shunt.
D. Waiting until age 2 risks irreversible pulmonary hypertension (Eisenmenger physiology); catheterization is not the definitive treatment of an AVSD and is used only selectively to assess pulmonary vascular resistance.
key_concept:
Down syndrome + infant heart failure = think AVSD, repair early.
  • Down syndrome: AVSD most common, then VSD and ASD
  • Large shunt signs: tachypnea, poor/interrupted feeding, failure to thrive, hepatomegaly, murmur
  • Complete AVSD: medical anti-failure therapy as a bridge, surgical repair in early infancy
  • Isolated large VSD: diuretics first, surgery if not improving after 6 to 12 months
  • Small asymptomatic VSD: observe, may close spontaneously
exam_pearl: For an isolated VSD in heart failure the first step is diuretics; for a Down syndrome infant (AVSD) the question asks definitive management, which is early surgery.

stem: Macrosomia baby has weak Moro reflex, what is the next step?
why_right: A "macrosomia baby" is at risk of shoulder dystocia, and a weak Moro reflex (on the affected side) after such a delivery points to brachial plexus injury, usually Erb palsy (C5 to C6). Most cases recover spontaneously, so the initial management is conservative: gentle immobilization of the arm across the body (avoid traction) and supportive care, followed by physiotherapy with passive range of motion. Surgery is reserved for infants with no recovery after a few months.
why_wrong_block:
B. Surgical nerve exploration/repair is considered only if function does not recover after about 3 to 6 months, not as the next step in a newborn.
C. Calcium supplements treat neonatal hypocalcemia (e.g., infant of a diabetic mother), which causes jitteriness or seizures, not a weak one-sided Moro.
D. Dextrose treats neonatal hypoglycemia, common in macrosomic infants of diabetic mothers, but that produces jitteriness, poor feeding, lethargy or seizures rather than a focal weak Moro.
key_concept:
Macrosomia + asymmetric/weak Moro = birth trauma (brachial plexus injury or clavicle fracture).
  • Erb palsy (C5 to C6): "waiter's tip" arm, absent Moro on that side, grasp preserved
  • Klumpke palsy (C8 to T1): claw hand, absent grasp
  • Management: immobilization, supportive care, physiotherapy
  • No recovery by about 3 to 6 months: refer for surgery
  • Hypoglycemia/hypocalcemia: global signs (jitteriness, seizures), not a one-arm deficit
exam_pearl: A focal one-sided reflex loss means a local (nerve or bone) injury; global depressed reflexes point to metabolic or CNS causes.
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0545).
Compiler note: A ✅. Macrosomic baby with weak/absent Moro suggests birth trauma, most commonly brachial plexus injury (Erb's palsy) after shoulder dystocia. Initial management conservative: immobilization of affected arm, supportive management, later physiotherapy. Surgery only considered later (3-6 months) if no recovery.

stem: Mother came with her child confirmed with chicken pox and shows you her photo with sure rash.
key_concept:
Varicella post-exposure prophylaxis depends on immune status.
  • Immunocompetent, already vaccinated or immune: observation
  • Immunocompetent, unvaccinated/unknown: varicella vaccine
  • Immunocompromised, asymptomatic (or susceptible pregnant woman): VZIG/IVIG
  • Immunocompromised, symptomatic: IV acyclovir
  • Child who already had typical, provider-verified chickenpox: counted as immune
exam_pearl: Live vaccine for the healthy susceptible contact; immunoglobulin only when a live vaccine cannot be given (pregnant or immunocompromised).

stem: Mother visited pediatric clinic before and confirmed diagnosis of chickenpox; the mother showed the doctor a picture of rash typical for varicella (infected before). Question was about varicella vaccine:
OptB: Postpone until the child is 2 years (or give after 2 years, could not remember)
key_concept:
Evidence of varicella immunity decides the dose.
  • Documented age-appropriate vaccination: immune
  • Laboratory evidence of immunity or confirmation of disease: immune
  • Provider-diagnosed or provider-verified typical varicella: counted as immune
  • Doubtful history: vaccinate (safe even if immune)
  • Prior varicella is never a contraindication to the vaccine
exam_pearl: Uncertainty favours vaccination: giving the varicella vaccine to an immune child is harmless, while missing a susceptible child is not.

stem: 18 month old, routine immunization; mother admitted that the child got varicella infection 2 months back, and showed the doctor a picture of the rash, and rash was typical of varicella (picture not provided, that is what the scenario said).
OptB: Postpone until the child is 2 years (or give after 2 years, could not remember)
why_right: The clues are an "18 month old" due for "routine immunization" whose past chickenpox rests on the mother's account and "a picture of the rash". Prior varicella is not a contraindication to the varicella vaccine, and a parental report with a photo is not laboratory confirmation of immunity. Since vaccinating a child who may already be immune is safe, this recall's key is to give the varicella vaccine as scheduled.
why_wrong_block:
A. Withholding fits only when immunity is accepted as proven (documented vaccination, laboratory evidence, or provider-verified disease); this key treats a mother's photo as not sufficient proof.
B. There is no reason to postpone to 2 years; live vaccines are delayed only after recent immunoglobulin/blood products, during moderate to severe illness, or with immunosuppression, none of which is present.
D. Immunoglobulin is for post-exposure prophylaxis in high-risk susceptible people (immunocompromised, pregnant, certain newborns); this is a healthy child, and IG given with the live vaccine would reduce its effectiveness.
key_concept:
Past chickenpox is not a contraindication to varicella vaccine.
  • Uncertain or unconfirmed history: vaccinate on schedule
  • True contraindications: anaphylaxis to a prior dose or component (e.g., gelatin, neomycin), immunosuppression, pregnancy
  • Defer live vaccine: recent immunoglobulin/blood products, moderate to severe acute illness
  • Not contraindications: mild illness, recent infection/convalescence, current antibiotics
exam_pearl: Recent infection or convalescence is a misconception, not a contraindication: vaccinate on schedule.

stem: A 5-month-old child whose 6-year-old brother has measles (the symptoms are not written, but the diagnosis is included). The question states that they spent a lot of time together. In short, the 6-year-old has symptoms, but the 5-month-old has no symptoms yet. The question asks: what would you give to the 5-month-old?
OptC: Nothing since he's under 6 months and doesn't need it
OptD: Measles drug something like that measles something
why_right: A "5-month-old" with close, prolonged contact with a sibling who has measles is a susceptible exposed infant, and infants are at high risk of severe measles. MMR is not given before 6 months, so the post-exposure prophylaxis for an infant under 6 months is immunoglobulin, given as soon as possible within 6 days of exposure.
why_wrong_block:
B. MMR is the post-exposure option (within 72 hours) for exposed people aged 6 months or older; at 5 months it is not given because maternal antibodies interfere and it is not licensed at this age.
C. Maternal antibodies may have waned by 5 months and cannot be relied on; young infants exposed to measles get severe disease and must receive prophylaxis.
D. There is no specific antiviral for measles prophylaxis; vitamin A is given to children who have measles (to reduce severity), not to prevent infection in an asymptomatic contact.
key_concept:
Measles post-exposure prophylaxis by age:
  • Under 6 months: immunoglobulin within 6 days
  • 6 to 11 months: MMR within 72 hours (or immunoglobulin within 6 days); an early MMR dose does not count toward the routine series
  • 12 months or older, susceptible: MMR within 72 hours
  • Immunocompromised or pregnant susceptible: immunoglobulin (no live vaccine)
  • Child with measles: supportive care plus vitamin A
exam_pearl: Age decides the answer: under 6 months always immunoglobulin, from 6 months MMR within 72 hours becomes possible.

stem: A term baby delivered by cesarean section, started to be tachypneic with nasal flaring and expiratory grunting. Chest X-ray showed fluid in the horizontal fissure. Blood pressure 60/35 mmHg, Heart rate 140 /min, Respiratory rate 65 /min, Temperature 36.6 °C, Oxygen saturation 92 %. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: The clues are a "term baby delivered by cesarean section" with tachypnea, nasal flaring and grunting, only mild hypoxia (SpO2 92%), and a chest X-ray showing "fluid in the horizontal fissure". This is transient tachypnea of the newborn: delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid, which is more common after cesarean delivery without labour. It is usually self-limiting within a few days with supportive care and oxygen as needed.
why_wrong_block:
A. Pneumonia needs infection risk factors (maternal fever, prolonged rupture of membranes, chorioamnionitis) or signs of sepsis, and the X-ray would show consolidation or infiltrates rather than fissural fluid; this baby is afebrile (36.6 °C) and no risk factors are given.
B. Meconium aspiration needs meconium-stained liquor, typically in a post-term or distressed baby, with patchy infiltrates and hyperinflation on X-ray; none of that is described.
C. RDS is a disease of preterm infants with surfactant deficiency, showing a diffuse ground-glass (reticulogranular) pattern with air bronchograms and worsening distress; this is a term baby with fissural fluid.
key_concept:
Neonatal respiratory distress: match the baby and the X-ray.
  • TTN: term, cesarean, fluid in fissures/perihilar streaks, resolves within days
  • RDS: preterm, surfactant deficiency, ground-glass with air bronchograms
  • Meconium aspiration: post-term, meconium liquor, patchy infiltrates with hyperinflation
  • Pneumonia: maternal fever/PROM, consolidation, signs of sepsis
exam_pearl: Same symptoms in a 27-week preterm with low saturations flips the answer to RDS; "term + cesarean + fissure fluid" is TTN.

stem: Pediatric age (9 y not sure) brought by his family because of nocturnal enuresis the issue is he has weight loss and polyuria (thirst) What to do?
why_right: The decisive clues are enuresis with "weight loss and polyuria (thirst)": new bed-wetting plus the osmotic triad in a school-age child is type 1 diabetes until proven otherwise. The immediate test is a random (or bedside capillary) glucose; a random glucose of 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or more with classic symptoms confirms diabetes, and the child should then be checked for ketones/DKA.
why_wrong_block: B. Urine culture is for suspected UTI (fever, dysuria, foul urine, pyuria or nitrites on urinalysis) and is not a first test; UTI does not explain weight loss and marked thirst.
key_concept:
Enuresis work-up: urinalysis for every child, then look for systemic causes.
  • Uncomplicated enuresis: urinalysis is the essential first test
  • Polyuria + polydipsia + weight loss: check glucose (type 1 DM)
  • Polyuria + polydipsia, dilute urine, no glycosuria: diabetes insipidus
  • Fever, foul urine, nitrite/pyuria: UTI, then urine culture
  • Constipation/encopresis, neurologic signs: look for spinal or bowel causes
exam_pearl: Plain enuresis means urinalysis; enuresis plus thirst and weight loss means glucose now.

stem: Pediatric age (9 y not sure) brought by his family because of nocturnal enuresis What to do?
key_concept:
Enuresis: urinalysis first in every child, then classify primary vs secondary.
  • Bedwetting is considered significant after about age 6
  • Secondary (new after a dry period): ask about stressors, UTI, DM
  • Primary: screen for systemic causes (DM, DI, sickle cell disease, seizures)
  • Recurrent UTI: renal ultrasound and VCUG
  • Spine deformity or abnormal neuro exam: MRI spine
  • A reference question with this exact scenario is keyed to Urinalysis.
exam_pearl: Glucose in the urine dipstick is what prompts a blood glucose test; urinalysis comes first and covers diabetes too.
